nodes.title: Delirium Prevention in Older Inpatients
nodes.summary: This section covers delirium in older inpatients, detailing recognition tools, non-pharmacological prevention strategies, medication review guidelines, and management for established episodes. It also addresses discharge planning and follow-up care.

children.title: Delirium Prevention in Older Inpatients — Overview
children.summary: This document is a synthetic test document and explicitly states it is not clinical guidance. It contains plausible recommendations regarding delirium prevention in older inpatients but warns against using them for patient care.
children.content:
> **SYNTHETIC TEST DOCUMENT — NOT CLINICAL GUIDANCE.** Written to exercise the
> ingest, indexing and retrieval pipeline. The recommendations below are
> plausible in shape but must never be used for patient care.

children.title: Background
children.summary: The passage states that delirium affects about 20% of older medical inpatients and up to 50% after hip fracture surgery. It notes this condition is linked to poor outcomes like longer stays and mortality, with one-third of episodes being preventable.
children.content:
Delirium affects roughly 20% of older medical inpatients and up to 50% of those
following hip fracture surgery. It is independently associated with longer
admission, functional decline, institutionalisation and mortality, and around a
third of episodes are preventable.

children.title: Recognition
children.summary: This section covers delirium recognition in older inpatients by detailing screening protocols using tools like the 4AT and explaining how to differentiate acute delirium from chronic dementia through assessment of onset and course.

children.title: Screening
children.summary: The passage details screening protocols for delirium in older inpatients aged 65 or over, recommending the use of the 4AT instrument. It notes that hypoactive delirium is a common and often missed presentation in this group.
children.content:
Screen every patient aged 65 or over within 24 hours of admission, and daily
thereafter on wards where the incidence exceeds 15%. The 4AT is the preferred
instrument: it requires no special training and takes under 2 minutes.

Hypoactive delirium is the more common presentation in the elderly and the more
frequently missed, because a quiet, withdrawn patient does not prompt review the
way an agitated one does.

children.title: Distinguishing Delirium from Dementia
children.summary: The passage distinguishes delirium from dementia by noting delirium's acute onset and fluctuating course with impaired attention, versus dementia's insidious and stable progression. It suggests obtaining a baseline assessment from a relative or carer for differentiation.
children.content:
Delirium has an acute onset over hours to days and a fluctuating course, with
impaired attention as the cardinal feature. Dementia is insidious and stable
day to day. The two coexist frequently, and a documented baseline from a
relative or carer is the most reliable way to tell them apart.

children.title: Non-Pharmacological Prevention
children.summary: This section covers multicomponent non-pharmacological delirium prevention for older inpatients. Topics include maintaining orientation and cognition, optimizing sleep and environment, and ensuring proper sensory function, mobility, and hydration status.

children.title: Non-Pharmacological Prevention — Overview
children.summary: Multicomponent interventions are discussed as a method for delirium prevention in older inpatients, noting they reduce incidence by about a third and show consistent evidence of benefit.
children.content:
Multicomponent interventions reduce incidence by about a third and are the only
approach with consistent evidence of benefit.

children.title: Orientation and Cognition
children.summary: This passage details non-pharmacological delirium prevention strategies for older inpatients, specifically addressing orientation and cognition by recommending visible clocks, staff reintroductions, family visits, and minimizing patient ward moves.
children.content:
Ensure a visible clock and calendar, reintroduce staff by name at each contact,
and encourage family visiting outside protected mealtimes. Avoid moving patients
between wards: each additional ward move raises the risk measurably.

children.title: Sleep and Environment
children.summary: The passage advises non-pharmacological strategies for improving sleep in older inpatients by dimming lights, using earplugs, and reducing routine overnight observations while explicitly advising against using hypnotics.
children.content:
Cluster observations to protect a continuous sleep period. Dim lighting
overnight, offer earplugs, and stop routine overnight observations in stable
patients. Do not use hypnotics as a sleep strategy.

children.title: Sensory, Mobility and Hydration
children.summary: This passage advises on delirium prevention by ensuring access to glasses and working hearing aids upon admission, mobilizing patients within 24 hours if safe, and daily review of fluid balance while removing urinary catheters promptly.
children.content:
Ensure glasses and working hearing aids are available from the first day of
admission. Mobilise within 24 hours where safe. Review fluid balance daily, and
remove urinary catheters at the earliest opportunity.

children.title: Medication Review
children.summary: The passage advises reviewing anticholinergic burden by stopping drugs like oxybutynin, amitriptyline, promethazine, and hyoscine. It also notes that benzodiazepines, opioids, and Z-drugs increase risk, recommending adequate pain treatment when opioids are necessary.
children.content:
Anticholinergic burden is the most modifiable pharmacological risk. Review
oxybutynin, amitriptyline, promethazine and hyoscine at admission and stop them
where possible.

Benzodiazepines, opioids and Z-drugs all raise risk. Where opioid analgesia is
required, treat pain adequately — undertreated pain is itself a stronger
precipitant than the analgesia used to control it.

children.title: Managing an Established Episode
children.summary: This section covers initial management steps for established delirium, including treating underlying causes and using non-pharmacological interventions. It also details when and how to use medications like antipsychotics, noting specific contraindications.

children.title: First Steps
children.summary: The passage advises identifying and treating delirium precipitants like infection or constipation. It also recommends verbal de-escalation and a familiar person as first-line interventions for distress.
children.content:
Identify and treat the precipitant: infection, retention, constipation, pain,
hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance or drug withdrawal. Delirium is a symptom, and
sedating the patient without finding the cause treats the observer rather than
the patient.

Verbal de-escalation and the presence of a familiar person are first-line for
distress.

children.title: When Medication Is Considered
children.summary: The passage advises reserving antipsychotics for severe distress or danger, specifying haloperidol use and duration limits. It cautions against using antipsychotics in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia, recommending lorazepam instead.
children.content:
Reserve antipsychotics for a patient who is a danger to themselves or others,
or whose distress is severe and unresponsive to non-pharmacological measures.
Use haloperidol 0.5 mg orally, reviewed after 2 hours, for no more than 5 days.

Avoid antipsychotics entirely in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy
bodies, where they may precipitate severe extrapyramidal deterioration. Use
lorazepam instead in those patients, and in delirium tremens.

Every antipsychotic prescription must carry a stop date at the point of
prescribing. Continuation on discharge is a common and avoidable harm.

children.title: Discharge and Follow-Up
children.summary: The passage advises documenting an episode's precipitant and resolution in the discharge summary. It also notes that persistent cognitive impairment at three months requires formal assessment rather than being linked to admission.
children.content:
Document the episode, its precipitant and its resolution in the discharge
summary. Persistent cognitive impairment at 3 months is common and warrants
formal cognitive assessment rather than being attributed to the admission.
